source.title: State-Dependent Safety Failures in Multi-Turn Language Model Interaction
source.authors: Pengcheng Li; Jie Zhang; Tian-Wei Zhang; Han Qiu; Ke-Jun Zhang; Wei-Ming Zhang; Neng-Hai Yu; Wenbo Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The study measures refusal-direction projections during multi-turn attacks and reports that STAR suppresses the projection while safety failures occur. This bears on V3, but it does not derive the direction or intervene on it as the original method does.
record.gate_note: The study measures refusal-direction projections for STAR and two comparison attacks. It does not ablate or add the direction, convert ablation into a weight edit, train against ablation, test transfer, or evaluate reasoning models. STAR attack success rates and history-intervention results are recorded as findings outside the listed versions because they do not establish that the attacks work by suppressing the direction. Cited findings from prior work and candidate-selection values are excluded.
record.test_reason: On LLaMA-3-8B-IT, the study projects hidden states onto the Arditi et al. refusal direction during multi-turn jailbreaks (STAR, X-Teaming, ActorAttack). This is a new setting (multi-turn conversation) with a result on V3: whether successful attacks coincide with suppression of the direction. The evidence is observational only. There is no intervention on the direction and no training against its ablation.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that multi-turn safety failures arise from contextual state evolution driven by dialogue history, with monotonic drift away from the refusal direction and abrupt role-anchored transitions. They also state that refusal-projection monitoring alone is insufficient for detection, because benign multi-turn interactions also show low refusal activation. They give no numbers for that statement.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows prior work to project hidden states onto a refusal direction, but does not derive the difference-in-means direction itself or perform the original ablation/addition interventions. It measures direction projections during multi-turn interactions.
record.method_sensitivity: The projection outcome differs by attack method: STAR shows a monotonic decline, while X-Teaming and ActorAttack retain substantially positive projections. The paper also reports sensitivity of attack success to dialogue-history structure and STAR components, but those results do not test the refusal-direction claim.

fits_no_version.finding: STAR safety failure rates across five models on HarmBench and three models on JailbreakBench.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured multi-turn interaction causes safety failures in models robust to static prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Component ablations and dialogue-history perturbations (shuffle, truncation, keep-last-k, refusal injection) change attack success or compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-turn attack success depends on dialogue-history construction.

fits_no_version.finding: A t-SNE of final-layer states shows STAR moving from a refusal region to a compliance region in one large step, while baselines oscillate near the boundary (Figure 5). The regions are not the difference-in-means direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-turn jailbreaks differ in their latent-state trajectory geometry.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The refusal-direction evidence is observational: the paper does not intervene on the direction or establish that its suppression causes the attack outcome. Projection results are reported for one open-weight model; comparison-attack values are described qualitatively from a figure. No uncertainty estimates are given for the direction projections or most behavioral results, and the paper reports no general-capability check.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out under the 60-row limit. Other attack-method comparisons in Tables 1 and 3 are not included because they do not measure refusal-direction suppression; STAR's own success rates are retained as findings under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Causal claim that attacks work by suppressing the direction (no ablation or restoration of the direction during attacks); training against ablation for robustness; projections on models other than LLaMA-3-8B-IT; per-prompt link between projection and success.
No ablation or addition of the direction; no capability check.
No separation of harm judgment and refusal.

missing.what: X-Teaming and ActorAttack SFR on LLaMA-3-8B-IT (84.9%, 79.0%). These are needed to interpret the partial-attenuation rows r5 and r6 as attacks that succeed without full suppression.

record.verdict_notes: The projection analysis covers one model and the reported numbers are final-layer values only; the comparison attacks are reported from a figure. The authors assert, without data, that benign multi-turn conversations also show low refusal projection. If true, low projection is not specific to jailbreaks, which weakens any reading of r2–r4 as mechanism. I chose tranche T3 (new multi-turn setting) over the reader's T2. The measurement mirrors the original paper's analysis of adversarial suffixes, but in a new interaction regime.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is derived or ablated or added; no general-capability check.
No refusal-direction weight edit or released-model abliteration.
The study measures direction projections during attacks but does not causally isolate suppression of that direction; it does not train against ablation.
No comparison of one direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test.
No comparison of refusal training methods or training stages.
